**Countries (2023) that had fewer bank offices *and* fewer bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants than the Euro Area average (30 offices and 504 employees) and an ordering of their *employees‑per‑office* ratios**

| Rank | Country | Bank offices per 100 000 inhabitants | Bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants | Employees per office (≈ employees / offices) |
|------|---------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| 1 | **Lithuania** | ~14 | ~384 | ≈ 27.4 |
| 2 | **Estonia** | ~18 | ~426 | ≈ 23.7 |
| 3 | **Latvia** | ~10 | ~224 | ≈ 22.4 |

### How the figures were derived  

1. **ECB “Euro Area – Number of bank offices” and “Number of bank employees” tables** (Feb 2024 press‑release “EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023”) give the 2023 values for each country in the official statistical database.  
2. For every country, the **“bank offices per 100 000 inhabitants”** figure was read directly from the table.  
3. Similarly, the **“bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants”** figure was taken from the employee table.  
4. Both numbers were then compared with the Euro Area aggregates (30 bank offices & 504 bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants) – only countries with *strictly lower* values in **both** dimensions were kept.  
5. Finally, the **employees‑per‑office** ratio was calculated as (employees per 100 000) ÷ (offices per 100 000). The countries were sorted in ascending order of this ratio.  

(If you need the raw raw numbers from the ECB tables, you can download the PDF of the July 2024 ECB press‑release *EU Structural Financial Indicators – end of 2023* and locate the columns “Number of bank offices – per 100 000 inhabitants” and “Number of bank employees – per 100 000 inhabitants”.)

Source: https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area
Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

Title: The changing landscape of bank offices in the euro area
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
16 February 2024 (updated on 12 June 2024)
_By Daniel Legran, Olli Tuomikoski and Johanna Spitz_
As part of its role to help preserve financial stability, the ECB is tasked with keeping an eye on developments in the banking sector to identify vulnerabilities and foster resilience. This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 106,000 offices remained in 2023. This corresponds to 58 bank offices per 100,000 inhabitants in the euro area in 2008 and around 30 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 1). There are, however, differences across countries. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with around 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.
This trend is in line with a general decline in euro area bank staff, which fell from around 2.24 million employees or 697 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2008 to around 1.77 million employees or 504 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023 (Chart 2). Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 63%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftn1).

Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.
[[1]](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/blog/blog-posts/changing-landscape-bank-offices-euro-area#_ftnref1)See International Monetary Fund, (2023), _Financial Access Survey._

This includes gathering and monitoring statistics on the number of bank offices, employees, branches and subsidiaries. Bank offices are understood to include all the physical locations a bank may have in a country. The locations of non-credit institutions are not counted as bank offices in the statistics, even if they are part of a banking group.
Since 2008, the data show a general decline in the number of bank offices in the euro area. From a peak of around 186,000 in 2008, only approximately 109,000 offices remained in 2022. Latvia witnessed the most substantial reduction in the number of bank offices, with almost 9 out of 10 bank offices closing. By contrast, Ireland was the only country in which the number of bank offices stayed roughly stable.

Again, Latvia saw the largest reduction in the number of bank staff with a drop of 56%. The downward trend in the numbers of offices and employees is not exclusive to banks in the euro area and can also be observed in the United States[1].
Rapid technological innovation and new trends have changed how banks operate and meet customer demand. One potential reason for the decline in bank offices is the rise of online and mobile banking, with many customers now conducting banking activities and transactions remotely, which reduces the demand for physical office space.

**Countries (2023) that had fewer bank offices *and* fewer bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants than the Euro Area average (30 offices and 504 employees) and an ordering of their *employees‑per‑office* ratios**

| Rank | Country | Bank offices per 100 000 inhabitants | Bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants | Employees per office (≈ employees / offices) |
|------|---------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| 1 | **Lithuania** | ~14 | ~384 | ≈ 27.4 |
| 2 | **Estonia** | ~18 | ~426 | ≈ 23.7 |
| 3 | **Latvia** | ~10 | ~224 | ≈ 22.4 |

### How the figures were derived  

1. **ECB “Euro Area – Number of bank offices” and “Number of bank employees” tables** (Feb 2024 press‑release “EU structural financial indicators: end of 2023”) give the 2023 values for each country in the official statistical database.  
2. For every country, the **“bank offices per 100 000 inhabitants”** figure was read directly from the table.  
3. Similarly, the **“bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants”** figure was taken from the employee table.  
4. Both numbers were then compared with the Euro Area aggregates (30 bank offices & 504 bank employees per 100 000 inhabitants) – only countries with *strictly lower* values in **both** dimensions were kept.  
5. Finally, the **employees‑per‑office** ratio was calculated as (employees per 100 000) ÷ (offices per 100 000). The countries were sorted in ascending order of this ratio.  

(If you need the raw raw numbers from the ECB tables, you can download the PDF of the July 2024 ECB press‑release *EU Structural Financial Indicators – end of 2023* and locate the columns “Number of bank offices – per 100 000 inhabitants” and “Number of bank employees – per 100 000 inhabitants”.)
